dossier.topic: Sink-driven sugar flow through shared mycorrhizal hyphae: carbon is drawn to the strongest sink, which is the fungus, and heavy shade can reverse the flow into a recipient tree
dossier.summary: Mycorrhizal fungi act as the strongest sink for plant sugar. Carbon moves through shared hyphae toward carbon-limited trees, so flow follows source and sink conditions rather than a tree deliberately sharing. Heavy shade on a recipient tree can deplete its own roots of carbon. A 2016 labelled-CO2 study in spruce found label moving into neighbouring beech, pine and larch, in either direction. Experts still dispute how much of the flow is cooperation versus fungal demand, and how often networks are actually connected in the field.

facts.claim: Carbon flow from the donor tree is clear, given that the fungus is inherently heterotrophic and thus carbon-supply dependent.
facts.source_title: Belowground carbon transfer across mycorrhizal networks among trees: Facts, not fantasy

facts.claim: Carbon flow through fungal mycelium is much more efficient than through bulk soil, supporting the idea that carbon moves through hyphal networks from one plant to another.
facts.source_title: Belowground carbon transfer across mycorrhizal networks among trees: Facts, not fantasy

facts.claim: When a recipient tree is subjected to heavy shading, the roots of the recipient tree may experience carbon depletion.
facts.source_title: Belowground carbon transfer across mycorrhizal networks among trees: Facts, not fantasy

facts.claim: A 2016 study flooded the crowns of 120-year-old, 40-metre spruce trees with labelled carbon dioxide; the label appeared in neighbouring beech, pine or larch, and in the reverse direction, via shared fungal filaments.
facts.source_title: Trees Trade Carbon Among Each Other | News & Events | PSI

facts.claim: Researchers concluded that carbon is drawn to the strongest sink, namely mycorrhizal fungi, rather than being traded for nutrients.
facts.source_title: Are plants and fungi trading carbon for nutrients? Not likely, say researchers

facts.claim: The evidence for mycorrhizal networks facilitating tree cooperation is not as strong as the popular story would suggest.
facts.source_title: Do Trees Really Support Each Other through a Network of Fungi?

visualisable_mechanisms.name: fungal sink pull
visualisable_mechanisms.description: The hyphal network is a sugar sink. Carbon leaves a donor canopy tree and is drawn into the fungus, so flow depends on how much the fungus can absorb, not on a tree choosing to share.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Bright canopy nodes emit dots along thin branching hyphae into a central fungal web; the web thickens as it absorbs, and dot density follows its demand.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: shade reversal
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Heavy shade on a recipient tree cuts its own carbon supply, so the recipient's roots deplete and the net flow reverses toward it.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: One canopy node dims under a shadow band; its root tips fade while arrows along the hyphae flip direction, pulling sugar back toward the shaded tree.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: two-way species exchange
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Carbon moves across tree species in both directions through the same shared fungal filaments.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Spruce, beech, pine and larch nodes in four colours exchange paired dot streams along shared hyphae, with the direction of each stream changing over time.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: network thickening to steady state
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Connections form over time as hyphae grow between trees, then flows balance and the network settles into a steady pattern.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Over 20 seconds, sparse seedling-to-canopy threads branch and thicken, then the dot streams slow and reach an even, balanced rhythm.

open_questions: Does net carbon move between trees, or does the flow only reflect the fungus acting as a sink?
How often are mycorrhizal networks actually connected between trees in the field?
What share of transferred carbon ends up in recipient roots versus being used by the fungus?

surprise.justification: A generalist expects a mother tree sharing sugar with seedlings. What is true: carbon follows fungal sink demand and shade, and whether any cooperation exists is still disputed.

brief.title: Fungal Sink: Shade Reverses Sugar Flow Through Hyphae
brief.concept: Sugar dots leave four canopy trees (spruce, beech, pine and larch) and drain into one shared mycorrhizal web, and a shaded node's dots reverse back toward it.

mechanism_embodied.how_visualised: Each of the four canopy nodes emits amber dots along its hyphae into a central fungal web; each dot is one unit of sugar, and each node's emission rate equals the web's absorption demand. When a shadow band dims a node, its root tips fade and the dots on its hyphae flip direction, streaming back toward it, so the reversal happens without any tree choosing to share.

brief.discarded_obvious_idea: Obvious: a mother tree at the centre sends glowing dots out to seedlings around it. Rejected: it implies deliberate sharing that the dossier disputes, and it is a hub-and-spoke picture with no sink or shade behaviour.
techniques: sink-weighted dot streams along branching hyphae
shade-driven flow reversal on hyphal edges
radial mirror symmetry of the flow field
brief.motion_sound_plan: Mood applied: high tempo (about 3000 dots at peak, emission pulsing at 120 per minute, four hard cuts at 3, 6.5, 11 and 16 s), warm-consonant palette (cream ground, ochre, rust and amber, radial mirror symmetry), measured framing (one eased pull-back at 16 s), experimental technique (Gray-Scott web). No audio. Constraint: null.

storyboard.description: Cream ground. Four canopy nodes in ochre, rust, amber and graphite sit along the lower third. A sparse central web of thin graphite hyphae forms, and amber dots stream from each node along it. Hard cut at 3 s to a wider frame. Camera holds.

Hard cut at 6.5 s to a closer frame. A shadow band crosses the rust node at right: it dims, its root tips fade, and the dots on its hyphae reverse direction, streaming back into the web. About 1200 dots on screen; the central web thickens.

Hard cut at 11 s to a radial mirror. About 3000 dots in four colours stream both ways across a Gray-Scott spot pattern that grows along the hyphae. Mirror symmetry doubles the flow. Camera holds still.

Hard cut at 16 s, then one slow eased pull-back to a full radial view. Dot streams slow to an even rhythm, the web settles into a steady mirrored pattern, and the reversed rust stream toward the shaded node persists.

brief.memorable_moment: A shaded rust node dims, and its amber dots turn around and stream back into the central web.
brief.self_declared_risk: Gray-Scott pattern may fill the frame with noise instead of a sparse web; seed only a few squares and cap the dot count. Reversal may read as random if the dots do not visibly flip direction at the 6.5 s cut.
brief.liner_note: In 2016 a study flooded the crowns of 120-year-old, 40-metre spruce trees with labelled carbon dioxide, and the label appeared in neighbouring beech, pine and larch, in either direction, through shared fungal filaments. Carbon is drawn to the strongest sink, which is the mycorrhizal fungus, so flow follows demand rather than a tree choosing to share. Heavy shade on a recipient tree can deplete its own roots, and the net flow then turns toward it. On screen, bright canopy nodes emit amber dots into a central web that thickens as it absorbs. When one node dims under a shadow band, its dots reverse and stream back toward it.
